extracted.intended_audience: mathematics teachers and educators (school and university); curriculum designers; mathematicians involved in teaching
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for teaching mathematics at school and university levels, emphasizing connection with physics, concrete examples, modelling, intuition, and historically-motivated definitions rather than sterile axiomatic presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach mathematics as part of physics/experimental science
rubrics_metrics.description: "Mathematics is a part of physics. Physics is an experimental science, a part of natural science. Mathematics is the part of physics where experiments are cheap."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present mathematical ideas via experiments, physical intuition and observable phenomena; treat mathematical objects and results as connected to empirical models rather than purely abstract games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid scholastic abstraction divorced from reality
rubrics_metrics.description: "Scholastic mathematics that is cut off from physics is fit neither for teaching nor for application in any other science" and leads to hatred of mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not prioritize sterile axiomatic constructions that lack motivating examples or physical meaning; avoid definitions/theories presented solely for internal logical beauty without demonstrating relevance or applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete, visual examples and drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be able to visualise and draw objects (e.g., paraboloids, curves from parametric equations); failure to do so signals poor training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include tasks like sketching surfaces given by xy = z^2 or plotting parametric curves x=t^3-3t, y=t^4-2t^2; develop spatial intuition as an essential mathematical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach mathematics through observation, examples, and counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: The scheme of construction: consider objects and make observations in special cases, find limits, look for counter-examples, then formulate empirical discovery clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize exploration, conjecture formation, testing against counterexamples, and only then precise formulation and proof; show examples where naive extension fails (e.g., partition sequence example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize modelling and its limits (axioms as idealisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modelling idealises certain facts as 'absolutely' correct and uses formal logic, but these idealisations must be tested because small parameter changes can alter outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach how models are constructed, when their conclusions apply, and the need for empirical/observational checks; use examples (Malthus equation, weather forecasting) to show limitations of relying solely on formal deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warn against fetishising theorems and forgetting relative nature of axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: The absolutised model separates from reality; long formal deductions become less reliable and can mislead if not compared with observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to question assumptions, understand dependence on axioms/initial conditions, and not to treat theorems as absolute truths divorced from modelling context (example: uniqueness theorem's limited practical relevance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach external control of deductions by experiments/examples
rubrics_metrics.description: "The technology of combatting such errors is the same external control by experiments or observations as in any experimental science and it should be taught from the very beginning to all juniors in schools."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruct students to verify long calculations by numerical examples, geometric interpretation, and experiments (where possible) to detect mistakes and validate reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate definitions with historical/concrete origins rather than abstract axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions should be understandable and motivated; e.g., define groups via transformations historically rather than as abstract axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start from natural concrete notions (transformations, mappings, geometric constructions) and derive axiomatic properties as obvious consequences, rather than imposing axioms upfront.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physically meaningful definitions (determinant as oriented volume, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The determinant of a matrix is an (oriented) volume of the parallelepiped whose edges are its columns; telling students this 'secret' makes the theory clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present algebraic objects with their geometric or physical interpretations to build intuition (e.g., determinants, Jacobians, implicit function theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach commutativity and arithmetic via counting/areas rather than abstract axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: It is only possible to understand commutativity of multiplication by counting and re-counting soldiers by ranks and files or by calculating the area of a rectangle in the two ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hands-on, concrete demonstrations (arrays, area computations, partitioning cakes/apples) to justify arithmetic properties before presenting abstract proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer historically or geometrically natural definitions of manifolds
rubrics_metrics.description: A smooth k-dimensional submanifold of R^N is its subset which in a neighbourhood of every point is a graph of a smooth mapping... this is more useful than the long abstract axiom list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce manifolds as familiar geometric objects (local graphs in Euclidean space) and use Whitney's theorem to explain abstract equivalence, rather than beginning with abstract topological axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach important classical results and topics for their pedagogical value
rubrics_metrics.description: The theorem of classification of surfaces is a top-class mathematical achievement and should be presented (even in high school) to give correct impression of modern mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include material like classification of surfaces, Riemann surfaces, Abel theorem, elliptic integrals, Picard-Lefschetz ideas, and show their connections and significance rather than omitting them as 'advanced' or 'obsolete'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stress interconnections in mathematics (heterogeneous connections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discoveries of connections between heterogeneous mathematical objects (e.g., same function controls sum of four squares and pendulum motion) are central and emotionally significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design curricula and lectures to highlight surprising links across fields (number theory ↔ analysis ↔ geometry ↔ mechanics) to inspire students and show unity of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presenting mathematical achievement as mere sporting/technical exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern mathematicians sometimes present 'sporting achievements' as the last word; this does not contribute to society's appreciation and causes distrust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize results with conceptual significance, applications or deep connections over technical feats with little explanatory or practical value when choosing teaching examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach computational and plotting skills as part of the craft
rubrics_metrics.description: From older calculus traditions until Goursat, ability to solve concrete problems (like drawing curves) was considered necessary part of the craft of every mathematician.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include exercises on computation, sketching, parametric plotting, and interpretation of formulas geometrically; value these practical abilities alongside theoretical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be familiar with and use classical high-quality pedagogical texts
rubrics_metrics.description: The best and most important methodological mathematical books (Rademacher & Töplitz; Hilbert & Cohn-Vossen; Courant & Robbins; Polya; Klein; Hermite; Landau & Lifshitz) should be known and used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt and recommend classical pedagogical works, translate them where necessary, and use their approaches (heuristics, problem-solving orientation, historical context) in teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce advanced concepts via accessible routes appropriate to students' intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: teach Abel theorem to schoolchildren by avoiding axiomatics and staying close to physics, covering complex numbers, Riemann surfaces, fundamental groups and monodromy along the way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, present advanced theorems through problem-based, example-rich development that builds necessary concepts incrementally rather than via heavy abstraction.
